prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, showing how selection into exporting and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework meets the criteria I care most about: a clear explanatory model, tied to newly available firm-level data, with consequences well beyond one subfield. Melitz (2003) supplied a tractable model that explains documented facts such as exporter premia, why only some firms export, and why trade liberalisation reallocates activity toward more productive firms. Helpman's firm-level work (for example with Melitz and Yeaple on exports versus FDI) broadens that model into a general account of how firms organise across borders. This pairing of new micro-data facts with a framework that explains them is what I value. It has produced a large and testable empirical literature, been applied in macro and labour settings, and informed trade-policy evaluation. After more than twenty years of replication and extension, maturity is not a concern. The two-name attribution is also relatively clean, which is unusual among the shortlisted candidates. Among the shortlisted entries, B010 has the broadest top-three support at opening, but I do not treat that as scientific merit. My case rests on the contribution itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and distinctiveness. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and Hopenhayn on firm dynamics, documented key facts or built closely related models, and none of them is on the credited list, so a two-name citation leaves out real precursors. The quantitative size of the selection and reallocation gains also depends on parametric assumptions, such as Pareto productivity draws, and some later empirical work questions it. The committee must therefore be satisfied that the citation honours the conceptual framework rather than any particular welfare number. There is also a legitimate question of how far this is a separate discovery from the new trade theory recognised in 2008.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B010 sixth and asks whether firm heterogeneity is a distinct advance beyond the new trade theory recognised in 2008. He also asks whether Redding or the Bernard-Jensen exporter facts should be included.
responses.response: I take the Krugman overlap seriously, but I think the two are distinct. The 2008 work centred on scale economies, love of variety and intra-industry trade among representative firms. The Melitz-Helpman line changes the unit of analysis to the firm and adds a selection and reallocation channel with its own testable predictions, such as exporter premia, entry and exit, and within-industry productivity gains. That is a different mechanism, not a refinement of the same one. On Redding, I agree he is influential, but his main contribution is on the quantitative and spatial side, which builds on this base. Including him would widen the citation beyond the core discovery. Bernard and Jensen documented key exporter facts, but they are not on the credited list, so I would draft the citation around the framework that explains those facts rather than try to credit them.

responses.point: Enflo ranked B032 first, with Autor, Hanson and Katz. She notes that credit splits between the task and skill framework and the trade-shock empirics. She ranked B010 third and flags antecedent claims from Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and from Hopenhayn.
responses.response: On B032 we are close in substance. I ranked it third and proposed only Autor and Hanson, because the ballot mixes two strands. Your point that Katz anchors the long-run skills-technology framework is fair, and I could accept that choice as a defensible alternative to mine. But it shows why the attribution is harder than for B010: the committee would have to decide which strand it is rewarding before it can name people. On antecedents, I agree they matter, and I share your concern about quantitative gains being model-sensitive. My answer is that a prize citation can reward the integrating framework without implying priority over every earlier empirical fact. That is also how I read the data-discovery-plus-explanatory-framework logic in recent prizes. I would keep the citation focused on selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B037 first, proposing Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He argues that nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are used daily in central banks and need no further confirmation.
responses.response: I agree the influence on practice is very large, and I do not dismiss the framework. My difficulty is attribution under the three-name limit. Your own opening acknowledges that Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler also made major contributions, so any triad is a judgment call and could fairly be contested. The post-2021 inflation also raised questions about the baseline model's performance that I would want addressed in a citation. B010 has a cleaner credit structure and a more settled empirical record. That is why I ranked B037 sixth and not first, though I accept that reasonable members weigh policy influence more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B019 first. He argues that Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 collateral-constraint mechanism is foundational for macro-finance, that the two-person attribution is clean, and that Gertler and Gilchrist's accelerator work extends it.
responses.response: I agree the two-name attribution is cleaner than for most macro candidates, and the post-2008 relevance is real. I did not rank B019 in my top eight, for two reasons. As several members note, the 2022 prize covers neighbouring banking and crisis themes, and direct empirical identification of the amplification channel is harder than the theory's influence suggests. Coming from an empirical field, I give weight to evidence that a mechanism has been identified in data. For B010 the evidence is firm-level and extensive. For B019 it is more indirect. I would not oppose B019 on merit, but I would want the committee to be explicit about how it differs from the 2022 recognition.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the Helpman-Melitz framework a sufficiently distinct advance beyond the 2008 new trade theory prize, and how to word the citation around precursors not on the credited list.
Whether Redding should be treated as co-core. I have left him out because his contribution is more quantitative and later, but others weigh it differently.
How much of the quantitative selection and reallocation gains survives alternative distributional assumptions, since the empirical evidence is mixed on the size of the effect.

Whether B003 should be paired with B010 as a second part. The BLP attribution is a trio (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes), and the three-person total across the configuration would force a partial credit that I find unsatisfactory.
I rely on my own background knowledge of these literatures and have not independently verified citation, replication or policy-use claims.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors are not credited on B010, and my research field is labour economics and crime. I note only field proximity to the labour candidate B032 (an alternative), with no documented personal or co-authorship connection to its credited names.
